title: Queen Pokou
author: Légende baoulé (Côte d'Ivoire)
desc: La légende de la Reine Abla Pokou, qui donna son nom au peuple baoulé.

p: More than three hundred years ago, in the great Ashanti kingdom, in today's Ghana, there lived a princess called Abla Pokou.
She was the niece of the king. She was intelligent, generous and brave. The people loved her.
When the old king died, there was a terrible war in the kingdom. Two families wanted the throne. Many people were killed.
Pokou's brother was killed in the fighting. Pokou knew that her life and the lives of her people were in danger.
"We must leave," she said. "We must go west, to find a new land where we can live in peace."
So, one night, Queen Pokou left with her people. Thousands of men, women and children walked west through the forest.
The journey was long and very hard. They walked for days and weeks. They had little food. The enemy warriors followed them.
Pokou carried her only son on her back. He was a baby. She loved him more than anything in the world.
Finally, they arrived at a big river: the Comoé. The water was high and dangerous. There was no bridge. There were no boats. And behind them, they could hear the enemy coming.
The people were afraid. They asked the soothsayer what to do.
The soothsayer looked at the river for a long time. Then he said: "The spirit of the river is angry. It wants a sacrifice. It wants the most precious thing we have."
The people brought gold, jewels, beautiful cloth. But the river did not change.
Queen Pokou looked at her people. She looked at the children, tired and hungry. She looked at her baby.
With tears in her eyes, she lifted her son and gave him to the river.

At that moment, something extraordinary happened. Huge trees bent over the water and made a bridge. Some say it was hippopotamuses that lined up in the river. The people crossed safely to the other side.
When everybody was on the other side, the trees stood up again. The enemy arrived at the river, but they could not cross.
The people were safe. They looked at their queen. She was standing by the river, very still, very sad.
She said only one word: "Ba-ou-li." In her language, it means: "The child is dead."
From that day, her people took the name of her sacrifice. They became the Baoulé people.
They settled in the centre of Côte d'Ivoire, around the towns we now call Bouaké and Sakassou. Queen Pokou ruled them with wisdom for many years.
Today, the Baoulé people still remember their queen. Her story is told to children, so that they never forget the price of their freedom.
